narrative:
The model estimates there is a 73.2 percent chance you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt, and that risk is why your application was denied. Admission decisions are based on predicting your likelihood of succeeding in law school and ultimately passing the bar, and this prediction is too close to failure to justify acceptance.

The most important factor in this decision was your class standing in the third year of your undergraduate studies. Your rank placed you in the lowest tenth of your class, while students who are typically accepted sit around the sixth decile on average. This very low performance in the final, most advanced year of study is a strong signal that you struggled with the type of rigorous, cumulative material that the bar exam tests. It pushed the prediction heavily toward failure.

Your LSAT score, though slightly below the average of admitted students, actually helped you. A score of 36 compared to a typical 37 is not a major gap, and the model viewed it as a small point in favor of your ability to pass the exam. However, it was not enough to offset the damage from your third-year rank.

Your first-year class standing also contributed toward a failure prediction, though less strongly. Placing in the third decile, versus an average of six among accepted students, reinforced the pattern of academic struggle that began early and continued through your final year.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your LSAT score meaningfully, as this is the area where you can show growth. Additionally, consider retaking coursework or obtaining a post-baccalaureate record that demonstrates your ability to handle advanced material, then reapply with a stronger academic narrative.
